content: Approximately 70% of women experience perineal trauma following vaginal delivery, necessitating sutures. This can lead to complications such as pain, the need for suture removal, and superficial dyspareunia. The study aimed to evaluate the effects of different suture materials on both shortand long-term morbidity associated with perineal repair. The research included 18 randomized trials involving 10,171 women. The comparisons included catgut sutures versus standard synthetic sutures (nine trials), rapidly absorbing synthetic sutures (two trials), and glycerol-impregnated catgut sutures (two trials). Additionally, standard synthetic sutures were compared with rapidly absorbing synthetic sutures (five trials) and monofilament sutures (one trial). When comparing catgut sutures to standard synthetic sutures, the latter was associated with reduced pain within the first three days postpartum (risk ratio [RR] 0.83, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.76 to 0.90) and decreased use of analgesics up to 10 days postpartum (RR 0.71, 95% CI 0.59 to 0.87). Women with catgut sutures were more likely to require resuturing (15 out of 1201 women) compared to those with synthetic sutures (3 out of 1201 women) (RR 0.25, 95% CI 0.08 to 0.74). However, women with standard synthetic sutures were more likely to require the removal of unabsorbed suture material (RR 1.81, 95% CI 1.46 to 2.24). When standard synthetic sutures were compared to rapidly absorbing synthetic sutures, there were no significant differences in shortor long-term pain. However, one trial reported that fewer women in the rapidly absorbing suture group required analgesics at 10 days postpartum (RR 0.57, 95% CI 0.43 to 0.77). Additionally, fewer women in the rapidly absorbing suture group required suture removal compared to the standard synthetic suture group (RR 0.24, 95% CI 0.15 to 0.36). There were no significant differences between these groups in terms of long-term pain (three months postpartum) or dyspareunia at three months or six to 12 months postpartum. When comparing catgut sutures to glycerol-impregnated catgut sutures, most outcomes were similar, although the glycerol-impregnated catgut was associated with increased short-term pain. In one trial comparing monofilament sutures to standard polyglycolic sutures, no significant differences were observed for most outcomes. In conclusion, catgut sutures may result in increased short-term pain compared to synthetic sutures. There were minimal differences between standard synthetic sutures and rapidly absorbing synthetic sutures, although the latter required less frequent suture removal. For other suture materials, the evidence was insufficient to draw definitive conclusions. These findings should be interpreted alongside the related Cochrane review on suturing techniques.
